routes.description: Craig argues cumulatively that cosmology, fine-tuning, objective morality, Jesus' resurrection, and immediate religious experience make Christian theism more reasonable than atheistic skepticism.
routes.successCriteria: The cited considerations must remain sufficiently warranted after Millican's objections and must jointly bridge from generic causal or supernatural conclusions to the morally perfect Christian God.

bridges.description: The cumulative evidence proportionately supports the complete Christian-theist conclusion over skeptical atheism.
A finite universe requires a transcendent personal cause rather than an unexplained physical origin.
Life-permitting constants and initial conditions are better explained by cosmic intelligence than necessity or chance.
Objective moral values and obligations require grounding in a good personal lawgiver.
The accepted historical facts concerning Jesus are best explained by a divine resurrection.
Immediate experience of God can provide non-inferential justification for Christian belief.
Evil and limited divine disclosure are compatible with God's salvific purposes and therefore do not defeat the cumulative case.

routes.description: Millican argues that the specific Christian God hypothesis bears a strong evidential burden and remains underdetermined or disfavored by the scientific, historical, psychological, moral, and empirical record.
routes.successCriteria: Skepticism succeeds if Craig's evidence does not reliably distinguish the Christian God from natural, unknown, or rival supernatural explanations, especially given evil and divine hiddenness.

bridges.description: The total evidence fails to favor the omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect Christian God over skeptical atheism.
Culturally variable religious methods and experiences are unreliable without independent empirical checks.
Neither a cosmic beginning nor a timeless personal cause follows securely from current physics or ordinary causal intuition.
Fine-tuning probabilities and explanations remain underdetermined and do not establish an omniperfect Christian designer.
Moral realism and human value remain available without a divine commander or ontological grounding in God.
Dependent, partisan, discrepant texts and known psychology do not warrant a miraculous resurrection inference.
Evil, obscure evidence, and sincere nonbelief are empirically discordant with a perfectly good God seeking relationship.

sections.title: Burden, Method, and Reliability
sections.rationale: The parties dispute the comparative burden, the reliability of religious belief-forming methods, and when absent evidence supports skepticism.

sections.title: Cosmological Argument
sections.rationale: The beginning, causal principle, infinity arguments, physical evidence, and personal-cause inference receive the debate's most sustained engagement.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Design
sections.rationale: Both sides treat fine-tuning as potentially evidential while disputing probabilities, rival explanations, scope, and implications for Christian theism.

sections.title: Objective Morality
sections.rationale: The exchange centrally contests whether objective value and obligation exist, what objectivity means, and whether either requires God.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence
sections.rationale: Craig's specifically Christian conclusion depends materially on the historical facts and whether resurrection is their best explanation.

sections.title: Religious Experience, Evil, and Hiddenness
sections.rationale: Immediate experience supplies Craig's non-inferential route, while evil, divine obscurity, and sincere nonbelief supply Millican's principal contrary evidence.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe began to exist and therefore has an uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial, personal transcendent cause.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the universe began to exist... therefore the universe has a transcendent cause... thus were brought... to its personal creator

moves.attributionBasis: The span lies continuously within Craig's identified opening speech and follows his explicit first-argument signposting.

response.rationale: This is Craig's opening cosmological construction and therefore has no earlier selected target requiring response contact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism is recoverable, but 'nothing,' causation outside time, and the exhaustive abstract-object-or-mind distinction need sharper specification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited infinity examples and BGV result support dispute, but the span presents an absolute beginning and personal cause more strongly than its supplied warrants establish.

charity.alternative: An eternal or otherwise physically explained universe, including speculative quantum or multiverse models.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument treats abstract objects and an unembodied mind as exhaustive nonphysical candidates without defending that exhaustiveness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core syllogism is valid, but the cause-to-personal-mind bridge and timeless causal relation remain materially implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Craig supplies philosophical examples and a named cosmological theorem, but extends them beyond the expressly stated expansion-boundary result.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it clearly and substantially advances the adopted cosmological case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances a central bridge from cosmic origin to a personal creator.

representationalCharity.rationale: The treatment of atheistic alternatives compresses the live range of physical and unknown-cause possibilities into a weakly defended dichotomy.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 95-257 contain the infinity argument, BGV appeal, causal syllogism, divine-attribute derivation, and personal-cause inference.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The extremely narrow life-permitting range of constants and initial conditions is best explained by design rather than physical necessity or chance.

sourceSpan.excerpt: only three possible explanations... physical necessity chance or design... therefore it is due to design

moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly labels this as his second argument during his uninterrupted opening presentation.

response.rationale: This is the initial fine-tuning constructive, presented before Millican offers any selected response target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The design inference is clear, but the probability space and scope of the allegedly exhaustive explanatory alternatives are not specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The existence of narrow life-permitting ranges supports inquiry, but the move asserts comparative probabilities without establishing their measure or excluding deeper laws and selection effects.

charity.alternative: Physical necessity, chance, and nondesign explanations of life-permitting constants and quantities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiverse selection and unknown deeper physical explanations are not independently evaluated before the alternatives are declared exhausted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive route is intelligible, but the explanatory trilemma and chance comparison rely on material unstated bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific types of fine-tuning are identified, yet no probability measure or representative quantitative case is defended within the span.

responsiveness.rationale: The opening move coherently advances the chosen design route without an earlier target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central designer bridge, though not by itself the full Christian conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states rival categories intelligibly but weakens them by omitting live deeper-law and observer-selection qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 258-323 state the constants and quantities, narrow life-permitting range, explanatory trilemma, pattern analogy, and design conclusion.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because objective moral values and duties exist but would not exist without God, their reality entails the existence of a good God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if God did not exist objective moral values and duties would not exist... objective moral values and duties do exist... therefore God exists

moves.attributionBasis: Craig identifies this as argument three and delivers the entire syllogism in his opening speech.

response.rationale: This move introduces the moral syllogism before Millican's selected objections and is therefore structurally constructive.

precisionFindings.rationale: Craig defines objective as belief-independent, but moves between values, duties, bindingness, and naturalism without fully distinguishing them.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is presented as logically inescapable although the God-dependence premise is supported mainly by one evolutionary account and an asserted absence of alternatives.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic accounts on which moral judgment is biologically and socially conditioned.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reconstruction does not address secular realist, Kantian, consequentialist, or reasons-based accounts of value and obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The syllogistic form is valid, but the key bridge from belief-independent normativity to a divine ground remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Moral experience and quoted authorities support the premises only partially and do not exclude major secular accounts.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it presents a clear route from moral experience to God.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally seeks to establish the creator's goodness and moral authority.

representationalCharity.rationale: It substantially weakens the live atheistic alternative by treating evolved moral psychology as if it exhausted secular moral ontology.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 324-406 contain both premises, the definition of objectivity, evolutionary examples, moral-experience analogy, and conclusion.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and origin of the disciples' resurrection belief are best explained by God's raising Jesus from the dead.

sourceSpan.excerpt: three facts recognized by the majority of historians... there just is no plausible naturalistic explanation... Jesus rose from the dead

moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this argument four and presents the three facts and explanatory conclusion continuously.

response.rationale: This is the first selected resurrection argument and precedes Millican's historical objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three-fact inference is clear and bounded, though the comparative standard for 'best explained' remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Named scholarly judgments support parts of the factual base, but the move moves rapidly from disputed facts to the exclusion of natural explanations and a miracle.

charity.alternative: Body theft, apparent death, and other naturalistic accounts of the reported resurrection evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Only two traditional alternatives are named, while source dependence, legend development, and cognitive explanations are not compared.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is recoverable, but the decisive historical-facts-to-miracle bridge is substantially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Craig supplies three claims and scholarly attributions, but offers little source analysis or comparative likelihood assessment.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive directly advances a specifically Christian evidential route.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is central to bridging generic theism to the Christian God identified in the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges some natural explanations but treats their rejection as exhausting the serious alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 407-472 specify Jesus' authority claims, the three historical claims, limited natural alternatives, and the resurrection conclusion.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A sincere seeker can know that God exists immediately through personal experience, independently of inferential arguments.

sourceSpan.excerpt: you can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments simply by immediately experiencing him... draw near to God and He will draw near to you

moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces this as his fifth point and completes it before concluding his opening speech.

response.rationale: The immediate-experience claim is initially constructive and has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practical claim is clear, but 'experience of God,' sincerity, evidential immediacy, and the promise's scope remain insufficiently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical promise to sincere seekers rests on testimony and scripture without addressing conflicting experiences, error, or sincere nonbelief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move offers an intelligible non-inferential route but does not explain how the experience identifies its object or defeats error.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Biblical promise and reported experience provide relevant testimony but no independent reliability check.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive advances an adopted experiential route, though it is less developed than the four arguments.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports rational theistic belief but supplies a limited bridge to specifically Christian truth.

representationalCharity.rationale: Charity is not tested because the move does not represent or attack a developed live alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 473-509 distinguish experience from argument, quote John Hick and scripture, invoke sincere seeking, and state the rational conclusion.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The specific Christian God hypothesis bears a strong burden because religious methods yield conflicting culturally inherited beliefs while minds and cognition are evidentially tied to physical systems.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if some method of acquiring beliefs leads to lots of different and conflicting beliefs then that method obviously cannot be relied on... a very strong burden of proof

moves.attributionBasis: The span is Millican's uninterrupted opening case after the chair expressly introduces him.

components.text: Immediate religious experience is a reliable way of identifying God.
Sincere seeking is promised to make God's existence evident.

response.rationale: Millican directly challenges experiential reliability through conflicting religions and physical dependence, but does not yet answer Craig's sincerity promise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Christian hypothesis and reliability test are explicit, though the numerical probability illustration and generalization across religious methods are broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move marks its probability assignment as generous and supports skepticism, but the leap from diversity and physical dependence to a very strong prior burden remains contestable.

charity.alternative: Craig's Christian God hypothesis and his use of logic, evidence, scripture, and personal experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move initially generalizes common religious acquisition methods before Craig has distinguished his philosophical evidence from cultural inheritance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route from method unreliability and specific-hypothesis breadth to a stronger burden is coherent, with a bounded prior-probability gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Millican supplies cultural, psychological, historical, and mind-brain examples, though several empirical generalizations remain uncited within the debate.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive reliability component but leaves Craig's sincere-seeker promise unanswered in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks a central experiential bridge and establishes the skeptical route's evidential standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: It states the Christian hypothesis accurately but initially compresses Craig's mixed method into the general pattern of inherited religious belief.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 538-790 define the Christian hypothesis, compare religious and scientific transmission, discuss mind-brain dependence, and set the skeptical burden.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Craig's Kalam case is valid in form but unsupported in its causal premise, cosmic-beginning premise, and inference to an unembodied mind.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the argument is of course logically valid... I'm not persuaded by either of the premises... the idea that a mind might exist... is complete speculation

moves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly turns to the Kalam argument and sustains the critique through the end of the cosmology portion of his opening.

components.text: The universe or global physical reality began to exist.
Whatever begins to exist must have an efficient cause.
The cause must be a personal unembodied mind.

response.rationale: The span separately challenges every indispensable cosmological component and explains why each defect blocks Craig's personal-creator conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: Millican carefully distinguishes local from global universe, material from efficient cause, and logical possibility from current physical evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move repeatedly emphasizes scientific uncertainty and presents unknown causation as more plausible rather than certain.

charity.alternative: Craig's Kalam syllogism, BGV appeal, infinity objection, and personal-cause inference.
charity.decisiveQualification: Millican acknowledges the syllogism's validity and the conditional scope of BGV before disputing its premises and extensions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The critique cleanly separates validity, premise support, whole-part scope, physical uncertainty, and the personal-cause inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It uses specific cosmological distinctions and Vilenkin's qualification, with some dependence on broad claims about current theory.

responsiveness.rationale: Every indispensable component of Craig's cosmological argument receives explicit and consequential contact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the complete central cosmological bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig's argument is reconstructed accurately, including its valid form and scientific rationale, before being criticized.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 791-999 address causal experience, quantum cases, composition, relativity, BGV, infinity, physical uncertainty, and the unembodied-mind inference.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Craig has not shown that belief-independent moral standards require God, because prominent secular moral theories reject mere majority preference.

sourceSpan.excerpt: atheists who take morality seriously... are very unlikely to think that what is right and wrong is just a democratic matter... specify a precise sense

moves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly marks this as his treatment of Craig's moral argument in his opening speech.

components.text: Belief-independent objective morality cannot exist without God.
Objective moral values and duties actually exist.

response.rationale: Millican challenges the decisive God-dependence premise with secular alternatives but postpones a fuller treatment of moral ontology and evil.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection identifies the disputed definition and distinguishes belief independence from democratic acceptance.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Millican frames the challenge as doubt and requests further specification rather than claiming to have settled moral ontology.

charity.alternative: Craig's definition of objective morality as valid and binding independently of belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Millican quotes the operative definition and contests its alleged implication rather than replacing it with simple subjectivism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The secular counterexamples directly undermine the asserted equivalence between atheism and belief-dependent morality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named families of secular ethics provide relevant countermodels, although their ontological grounding is only sketched.

responsiveness.rationale: The decisive God-dependence premise is contacted, while the second premise and full ontology remain untreated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks the central moral-grounding bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig's published definition and intended independence condition are represented accurately before challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1000-1051 discuss the ambiguity of objectivity, secular utilitarian, Kantian, and Humean standards, and pose a two-part challenge.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Millican must justify atheism, while religious diversity does not defeat Craig's use of logic, evidence, and experience and absent evidence is not automatically evidence of absence.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there is no one method which is common to all religions... my method this evening is logic and evidence plus personal experience... absence of evidence is not necessarily evidence of absence

moves.attributionBasis: The chair introduces Craig's first rebuttal, and Craig expressly addresses Millican's burden and reliability case.

components.text: Religious methods share a conflict-producing reliability defect.
The specific Christian claim bears an overwhelmingly strong burden.
The observed evidence is too sparse for the Christian hypothesis.

response.rationale: Craig directly answers Millican's common-method, burden, and absent-evidence components and states the conditions under which absence would be probative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move distinguishes absence of evidence from evidence of absence and states the expected-evidence condition clearly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional account of absent evidence is well calibrated, but the claim that the existing five considerations obviously exhaust expected evidence is stronger than shown.

charity.alternative: Millican's conflict-based reliability argument, asymmetrical burden, and inference from evidential absence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Millican argued that similar methods are unreliable, not that every religion literally uses one identical method.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expected-evidence test is coherent, though the burden dispute and transition from five alleged data points to sufficiency remain contestable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Pluto and planet analogies clarify the principle, but application to divine intentions lacks independent support.

responsiveness.rationale: All indispensable parts of Millican's methodological challenge receive explicit contact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the skeptical route's central reliability and burden bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It initially recasts Millican's similar-method claim as a demand for one identical method, weakening the stated reliability argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1063-1161 contain the burden dispute, genetic-fallacy response, method distinction, absence analogies, and expected-evidence test.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: BGV and Vilenkin support an absolute beginning, quantum vacua are not nothing, the causal principle is not compositional, and substance dualism makes a personal cause possible.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the short answer is yes... the vacuum is a sea of fluctuating energy it is not nothing... the argument isn't reasoning from composition... some sort of substance dualism

moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly returns to the first argument and answers Millican's cosmological objections in sequence.

components.text: BGV does not establish the beginning of global physical reality.
Experience and quantum cases fail to warrant universal causation.
The causal inference commits a composition error.
An unembodied personal cause lacks evidential support.

response.rationale: Craig answers every indispensable objection with a quotation, metaphysical distinction, or dualist countermodel and reconnects them to the creator conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The replies are individually clear, but 'beginning,' quantum causation, nonbeing, and substance dualism still operate across disputed scopes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The fuller Vilenkin quotation and vacuum distinction improve support, though Craig still treats present cosmology and dualism as more decisive than demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Millican's contracting cosmology, quantum analogy, composition objection, and embodied-mind evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig quotes the instability qualification and separates material from efficient causation before responding.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response is systematically organized and removes the composition charge, with residual gaps in timeless causation and the dualist inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies specific Vilenkin and philosopher-of-science quotations and conceptual distinctions, though the dualism portion is comparatively compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: Every indispensable component of Millican's selected cosmology target is expressly contacted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The response directly defends the complete central cosmological bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican's principal objections are accurately identified and answered in their qualified forms.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1164-1334 contain the full Vilenkin context, quantum-vacuum distinction, composition response, metaphysical causation claim, and dualist defense.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Secular ethical theories presuppose unexplained intrinsic human value and cannot make obligation intelligible without a personal moral prescriber.

sourceSpan.excerpt: all of those presuppose that human beings have some sort of intrinsic value... prescriptions require prescribers... without a moral lawgiver moral obligation is unintelligible

moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly turns from cosmology to Millican's objections to the moral argument.

components.text: Secular theories provide belief-independent standards without God.
Craig must explain what divine grounding adds to moral obligation.

response.rationale: Craig engages both the secular-theory counterexamples and their proposed grounding by distinguishing value from obligation and invoking a prescriber.

precisionFindings.rationale: The value-versus-obligation distinction is useful, but 'prescription,' 'obligation,' and intrinsic value are treated as if their divine dependence were definitional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move confidently declares secular obligation unintelligible without comparing impersonal reasons, contractual, Kantian, or realist accounts.

charity.alternative: Utilitarian, Kantian, and Humean accounts of secular value and obligation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The response treats all secular theories as presupposing unexplained human value despite Millican's broader point about belief-independent standards.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response identifies distinct questions of value and duty, but the premise that prescriptions require a person is asserted rather than derived.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies a clear conceptual warrant but no comparative defense against the secular theories already identified.

responsiveness.rationale: Both indispensable parts of Millican's moral challenge receive direct contact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly defends the central divine-grounding bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Secular alternatives are recognized but compressed into a single unexplained-value objection that does not preserve their strongest grounding claims.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1336-1363 distinguish intrinsic value from obligations and present the moral-prescriber response to Millican's secular alternatives.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning conditionally invites a designer explanation, but unknown probability spaces, immature physics, multiverses, anti-God symmetry, and divine omnipotence block Craig's stronger inference.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if there is a physically inexplicable coincidence... invites explanation in terms of a cosmic scale designer... but I also see good reason for caution and modesty

moves.attributionBasis: Millican expressly announces his fine-tuning response and develops it continuously through the theological implications.

components.text: Life-permitting constants have a well-founded low probability under chance.
Necessity, chance, and design exhaust the explanatory alternatives.
Design supports the morally perfect Christian God.

response.rationale: Millican concedes the conditional evidential core, then separately attacks the probability, explanatory exhaustion, and Christian-scope components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The designer concession is expressly conditional, and objections are carefully separated by probability, physics, morality, power, time, and space.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The span repeatedly acknowledges genuine intrigue and states what stronger future evidence would be needed while emphasizing current uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Craig's design inference from narrow life-permitting constants and quantities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Millican grants that a genuinely inexplicable coincidence would naturally invite a cosmic designer explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response combines a clear conditional concession with independent objections to probability, rival explanations, and theological scope.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It offers concrete physical unknowns, multiverse selection, temporal and spatial proportions, and anti-God symmetry, with some speculative projections.

responsiveness.rationale: Every indispensable component of Craig's design inference receives explicit contact, including the decisive explanatory comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the full central fine-tuning bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig's strongest conditional design case is explicitly conceded before its limits are developed.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1379-1553 cover the conditional concession, sample-size problem, deeper physics, multiverses, anti-God, omnipotence, inefficiency, empty space, and aliens.

moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Infinite-set subtraction creates no contradiction, present cosmology remains provisional, causal intuition lacks evidence at creation ex nihilo, and unknown causes are not exhausted by abstract objects and minds.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there's absolutely nothing mysterious or contradictory... where is your evidence that nothing can come into existence without a cause... there may be all sorts of things we've never thought of

moves.attributionBasis: Millican announces the infinity reply and then expressly returns to Craig's cosmological rebuttal.

components.text: Actual infinity yields contradictory real-world subtraction results.
Current cosmology strongly warrants an absolute beginning.
Creation without a cause is metaphysically absurd.
Abstract object or disembodied mind exhaust the nonphysical candidates.

response.rationale: Millican contacts all decisive rebuttal components and explains why each still fails to establish Craig's transcendent personal cause.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move gives an exact account of why subtraction is undefined and distinguishes empirical openness from dogmatic naturalism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Millican expressly treats unknown alternatives and future physics as possibilities and does not claim a demonstrated uncaused origin.

charity.alternative: Craig's real-infinity contradiction, contemporary-physics appeal, metaphysical causal principle, and dualist candidate inference.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move accepts that the quantum vacuum is not nothing and that mental properties are not identical with physical properties.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The infinity explanation is rigorous and the remaining replies consistently apply the stated empiricist standard.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Mathematical explanation and scientific caution are well supported, though the computer analogy only sketches a nondualist mind account.

responsiveness.rationale: Every indispensable component of Craig's cosmological rebuttal is explicitly contacted and tied to its defeating consequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the entire central cosmological route.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig's qualifications about the vacuum and mental properties are expressly preserved before disagreement.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1554-1696 present the Cantorian subtraction explanation, scientific provisos, causal-evidence challenge, candidate-exhaustion objection, and computer analogy.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Limited divine evidence does not support atheism because God may know that greater disclosure would not bring more people freely into saving relationship.

sourceSpan.excerpt: giving any more evidence of his existence would not lead more people to love and come to know his salvation... they might have come to resent a God

moves.attributionBasis: Craig opens his second rebuttal by returning directly to Millican's evidential-absence argument.

components.text: A relational God should provide clearer public evidence of existence.
Conflicting religious methods undermine experiential reliability.

response.rationale: Craig directly proposes a salvific explanation for limited evidence but does not contact Millican's independent conflict and method-reliability argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is repeatedly qualified as a possibility about divine purposes rather than asserted as known fact.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited modal conclusion matches the speculative divine-purpose warrant, although it has little independent evidential support.

charity.alternative: Millican's claim that a relational God's existence should be more evident.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig accurately treats the claim as an expected-evidence judgment rather than as a deductive disproof.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed purpose is logically compatible with hiddenness, but compatibility alone does not make it a likely explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The response supplies a possible divine motive but no evidence that greater disclosure would reduce salvation.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive expected-evidence component while leaving the independent reliability component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially defends the central hiddenness bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican's expected-evidence objection is fairly identified, with only minor compression of its broader empirical basis.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1705-1745 state the expected-evidence criterion and offer salvation, free relationship, and possible resentment as explanations of limited disclosure.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Millican's mathematical account does not remove the absurdity of real infinite collections, while current physics, causation, and substance dualism continue to support a personal cosmic cause.

sourceSpan.excerpt: you can't stop someone from taking away a certain number of coins... the evidence of current physics supports the fact... I see no problem... an immaterial spiritual consciousness

moves.attributionBasis: Craig moves explicitly from hiddenness back through Millican's infinity, physics, causation, and mind objections.

components.text: Undefined infinite subtraction is harmless and noncontradictory.
Provisional physics cannot warrant a confident beginning conclusion.
The causal principle lacks relevant creation evidence.
Mind-body evidence undercuts a disembodied cause.

response.rationale: Craig explicitly revisits all principal counterreply components and reconnects them to the cosmological conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The real-collection objection is clear, but the treatment of zero, identity of infinite quantities, and substance dualism remains conceptually compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Craig properly limits the physics claim to current evidence, but presents the metaphysical and dualist components more confidently than their supplied arguments warrant.

charity.alternative: Millican's Cantorian account, provisional-physics caution, evidential causal challenge, and embodied-mind objection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig recognizes that Millican accepts mental properties and rejects epiphenomenalism rather than treating him as a reductive materialist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response is connected and targeted, though the mathematical objection and move from non-epiphenomenalism to substance dualism remain incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Current-physics support is relevant, but the metaphysical and philosophy-of-mind claims receive limited comparative defense.

responsiveness.rationale: All indispensable components of Millican's counterreply receive direct contact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly defends the central personal-cause route.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican's mathematical and empirical qualifications are accurately described before Craig disputes their consequences.

moves.evidenceBasis: Events 1747-1829 address real subtraction, zero, current cosmology, vacuum causation, dualism, and the possibility of an immaterial creator.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning probabilities remain meaningful, diverse cases resist future-physics dissolution, and objections from inefficiency, empty space, aliens, or anti-God do not defeat a cosmic-designer inference.

sourceSpan.excerpt: compare the possible range... to the life permitting range... cases of fine tuning are multiple and diverse... none of these 9... take seriously the problem

moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly counts and answers Millican's fine-tuning objections in his second rebuttal.

components.text: The relevant cosmic probability comparison is ill-defined.
Future physics or multiverses remain live rivals.
Fine-tuning cannot distinguish a good God from anti-God.
Omnipotence, cosmic waste, and alien life undermine Christian design.

response.rationale: Craig expressly responds to the probability, future-physics, moral-scope, efficiency, spatial, and alien-life objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: The response distinguishes the designer conclusion from God's moral and infinite attributes, but the possible-range measure remains underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Craig appropriately denies that fine-tuning alone proves moral perfection or infinite power, while still treating its probability basis more firmly than defended.
